questions.q: In which year did Japan forcibly incorporate Dokdo into Shimane Prefecture during the Russo-Japanese War?
questions.fact: Japan forcibly incorporated Dokdo into Shimane Prefecture in [[1905]].
questions.explain: Five years after the Korean Empire's Imperial Edict No. 41 of 1900, Japan used wartime conditions to seize the island unilaterally.
questions.tip: This was the long-awaited first question.

questions.q: What name did the Joseon fisherman An Yong-bok use for Dokdo in Japan?
questions.fact: An Yong-bok called Dokdo [[Jasando]] at a hearing in Japan.
questions.explain: The Murakami family documents from the Oki Islands identify Jasando with Usando and Dokdo, making them important for comparing historical records.
questions.tip: Only 10% answered correctly. Many chose Usando, the name used in official Joseon records.
questions.deep: During his second journey to Japan in 1696, An Yong-bok called Dokdo 'Jasando' at the Hoki provincial office. The name resulted from transcribing the first character in Usando differently, and appears in the interrogation record kept by the Murakami family of the Oki Islands. The significance of this document is that a Japanese source challenges the claim by Japanese scholars that Joseon's Usando and present-day Dokdo were different islands.

wrong.0: This is the name in official Joseon records, but not the one asked for here.
wrong.2: This is the name in Imperial Edict No. 41 of 1900, about 200 years after An Yong-bok.
wrong.3: This nickname refers to the large number of gangchi, or sea lions.

questions.q: Which Japanese geography book of 1667 described Dokdo and Ulleungdo as Joseon territory?
questions.fact: The 1667 [[Onshu Shicho Goki]] placed Japan's northwestern limit at the Oki Islands.
questions.explain: It is described here as the earliest official Japanese record limiting Japan's boundary to the Oki Islands.
questions.tip: At 10%, this had the lowest correct-answer rate among the medium questions. The famous Dajokan Directive often overshadows it.
questions.deep: Saito Hosen, an official of Izumo Domain, compiled this geography book in 1667. After describing Ulleungdo and Dokdo, it states that Japan's northwestern boundary ends at this province, meaning the Oki Islands. The source presents this as the earliest official Japanese record drawing that boundary at Oki and thus placing Dokdo beyond it.

wrong.0: This document dates to 1877, 210 years later. Its fame attracted 41% of answers.
wrong.2: This was a reply to the shogunate's inquiry in 1695, not a geography book.
wrong.3: This incorporation notice dates to 1905, a different period.

questions.q: How many times has Japan proposed referring the Dokdo sovereignty issue to the International Court of Justice (ICJ)?
questions.fact: Japan proposed an ICJ referral in 1954, 1962 and 2012: [[three times]] in total.
questions.explain: The source interprets these proposals as an attempt to portray Dokdo as internationally disputed territory, under the appearance of seeking a peaceful resolution.
questions.tip: Many chose four times.
questions.deep: The three years are 1954, 1962 and 2012. The source explains that an ICJ case requires the parties' consent, so the proposed case cannot proceed if Korea does not agree. It interprets the repeated proposals as aimed less at a trial than at presenting Dokdo to the international community as a disputed area.

wrong.0: This remembers only the latest proposal, in 2012.
wrong.1: This remembers 1954 and 2012 but omits 1962.
wrong.3: This attracted 51% of responses. Mixing preliminary attempts with formal proposals inflates the total.

questions.q: What is the official name of the highest peak on Dokdo's Seodo (West Islet)?
questions.fact: The highest peak on Seodo (West Islet) is [[Daehanbong]], at 168.5 m.
questions.explain: Dokdo's highest point, at 168.5 m, bears the name 'Daehan,' meaning Korea.
questions.tip: The correct-answer rate was very low because many confused it with Usanbong on Dongdo (East Islet).
questions.deep: At 168.5 m above sea level, the summit of Seodo (West Islet) is Dokdo's highest point. The source says that Ulleung County's place-name committee officially named it Daehanbong in 2000 and named Dongdo's 98.6 m summit Usanbong. The name 'Daehan' at Dokdo's highest point carries symbolic meaning.

wrong.0: This is Dongdo's highest peak. The two names are often reversed.
wrong.2: This is not an existing peak name here.
wrong.3: Isabu's name is used in the road name Dokdo Isabu-gil.

questions.q: What directly caused An Yong-bok's first journey to Japan in 1693?
choices: He was sent as an official Joseon envoy
Japanese fishermen abducted him on Ulleungdo
He went voluntarily to negotiate over Dokdo
He was detained over a trade dispute
questions.fact: In 1693, Japanese fishermen took An Yong-bok from Ulleungdo to Japan after he was [[abducted]].
questions.explain: Even after being abducted, he firmly told the governor of Hoki that the islands were Joseon territory.
questions.tip: A fisherman's courage changed the course of history.
questions.deep: While fishing on Ulleungdo in spring 1693, An Yong-bok encountered Japanese fishermen, who seized him and took him to the Oki Islands. Despite being a captive, he asserted before the governor of Hoki that Ulleungdo and Dokdo were Joseon territory. The source says he eventually obtained a document from the shogunate to that effect.

wrong.0: He was a commoner, not a government official.
wrong.2: His voluntary journey was his second trip, in 1696.
wrong.3: The encounter concerned fishing, not trade.

questions.q: How deep is the water between Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet)?
questions.fact: The water between Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet) is [[less than 10 m]] deep.
questions.explain: Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet) are separate islets above the water but share a single volcanic base beneath it.
questions.tip: Rated easy, but only 16% got it right. One of our biggest surprises!
questions.deep: Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet) look like two separate islands. But the channel between them is about 151 m wide and less than 10 m deep. Under the sea, they are joined as parts of the same volcano. They are what remains of a single volcano that formed 4.6 million years ago. They are two islets above water, joined by the same volcanic structure below.

wrong.1: This range starts at 10 m, whereas the stated depth is less than 10 m.
wrong.2: You may be mixing this up with the flat seabed of the East Sea, about 2,000 m deep.
wrong.3: This does not match what we see: the two islands are linked under shallow water.

questions.q: Which French ship recorded Dokdo on Western maps in 1849?
questions.fact: The French whaling ship that first put Dokdo on Western maps in 1849 was the [[Liancourt]].
questions.explain: The alternative Western name 'Liancourt Rocks' for Dokdo comes from this vessel.
questions.tip: This question explains a name found on maps from third countries.

questions.q: On the map in the 1837 Hachiemon trial records, what color represents Japanese territory?
questions.fact: On the map in the Hachiemon trial records, Japanese territory is colored [[yellow]].
questions.explain: The Edo shogunate colored Japan yellow and Joseon's Ulleungdo and Dokdo red.
questions.tip: The contrasting colors make this a powerful visual example.
questions.deep: These records concern Hachiemon, a merchant from Hamada Domain who was executed after violating the ban on sea passage and trading illegally on Ulleungdo. In the attached directional map, Japanese territory is yellow and Joseon territory red; Ulleungdo and Dokdo are red. The source presents Dokdo's color on this Japanese map as visual historical evidence.

wrong.0: This is the color used for Joseon: the colors have been reversed.
wrong.2: This color is not used for the territories on this map.
wrong.3: This color is not used for the territories on this map.

questions.q: What is the road name on Dokdo's Seodo (West Islet)?
questions.fact: The road on Seodo (West Islet) is called [[Dokdo An Yong-bok-gil]].
questions.explain: Dongdo's road honors the Silla general Isabu. Seodo's road honors An Yong-bok, the Joseon fisherman.
questions.tip: These administrative addresses preserve names from 1,500 years of history.

questions.q: Why are the Murakami family documents from the Oki Islands important in the Dokdo sovereignty debate?
choices: They record Japanese fishermen working on Dokdo
They identify Jasando, Usando and Dokdo as the same island
They place Dokdo under Oki jurisdiction
They recognize An Yong-bok as a Joseon official
questions.fact: The Murakami family documents identify [[Jasando as Usando and Dokdo]].
questions.distractor: Dokdo as part of Oki jurisdiction
questions.explain: The source uses Japanese records to challenge the claim that Joseon's Usando and modern Dokdo were different islands.
questions.tip: This historical question received many responses on the channel.

questions.q: What is the contradiction between Japan's 'inherent territory' claim and its claim to have occupied ownerless Dokdo in 1905?
choices: Earlier Japanese control made incorporation unnecessary
Inherent territory cannot also be newly occupied ownerless land
Occupation of ownerless land is never a valid legal method
Japan had no treaty with the Korean Empire in 1905
questions.fact: If territory was already inherent, it did not need to be occupied as ownerless land: the two claims are [[incompatible]].
questions.explain: The question highlights an internal contradiction in Japan's stated reasoning.
questions.tip: Pointing out this contrast clearly works well in a live discussion.

questions.q: What is the main reason the waters around Dokdo are rich fishing grounds?
choices: Shallow water lets in abundant sunlight
Warm and cold currents meet in a frontal zone
The Chinese continental shelf supplies the nutrients
questions.fact: Dokdo's rich fishing grounds lie in a [[frontal zone]] where warm and cold currents meet.
questions.explain: Where warm and cold currents meet, plankton can grow abundantly.
questions.tip: A clear ocean-science question with a high correct-answer rate.

questions.q: What is Dokdo's approximate total land area?
questions.fact: Dokdo's total land area is about [[187,554 m²]].
questions.explain: This combines Dongdo (East Islet), Seodo (West Islet) and 89 smaller islands.
questions.tip: Although only about 6% of Yeouido's area, this small island group has great maritime value.

questions.q: Which Japanese domain officially replied that Ulleungdo and Dokdo were not under its jurisdiction?
questions.fact: The Japanese domain that denied jurisdiction over the islands in 1695 was [[Tottori Domain]].
questions.explain: The source points to a surviving document in which the nearby Japanese domain denied jurisdiction over the islands.
questions.tip: A difficult question: many confused it with Shimane.
questions.deep: In 1695, the shogunate asked when Ulleungdo had become part of Tottori Domain. Tottori replied that neither Ulleungdo nor Dokdo, nor any other such islands, belonged to the domain. The source treats this denial by a nearby Japanese domain as a direct basis for the following year's passage ban.

wrong.0: This confuses it with Shimane Prefecture, which issued the 1905 notice. It attracted 43% of answers.
wrong.1: The Oki Islands belonged to Matsue Domain, not Tottori.
wrong.3: Nagasaki handled foreign contacts but was not the domain in this exchange.

questions.q: Which part of Dokdo can ordinary tourists visit?
choices: Both Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet)
Only Dongdo (East Islet) is open to tourists
Only Seodo (West Islet) is open to tourists
Neither islet is currently open to the public
questions.fact: Ordinary tourists may land only on [[Dongdo (East Islet)]].
questions.explain: Dokdo opened fully to the public in 2005. Since then, 3.6 million Koreans have stepped onto the landing dock on Dongdo (East Islet).
questions.tip: Every visit shows Korea's effective control on the ground.

questions.q: How did Japan use Dokdo for military purposes during the Russo-Japanese War in 1905?
choices: Built a naval base and stationed a fleet
Installed a watchtower and undersea cables to watch Russian ships
Used the island as a prisoner-of-war camp
Fought a naval battle directly from the island
questions.fact: During the Russo-Japanese War, Japan installed [[a watchtower and undersea cables]] on Dokdo to monitor Russian ships.
questions.distractor: a naval base and a fleet
questions.explain: The source links these installations to Japan's military motive for seizing Dokdo in 1905.
questions.tip: A central historical question.

questions.q: What is Dokdo's postal code?
questions.fact: Dokdo's postal code is [[40240]].
questions.explain: The source presents the postal code as evidence that the Republic of Korea's administrative network reaches Dokdo, and claims that disputed areas cannot receive postal codes.
questions.tip: An everyday example of administrative sovereignty.
questions.deep: The source describes this as the five-digit code assigned alongside the 2015 address-system change. It interprets '40' as Gyeongsangbuk-do and '240' as the Ulleung County area. It further claims that international law prevents one country from assigning a postal code to disputed territory. These are claims retained from the supplied Korean text; see the editorial review notes.

wrong.0: This is a Seoul Gangnam-area code.
wrong.1: This is an Incheon-area code.
wrong.3: This is a Jeju-area code.

questions.q: What key evidence did An Yong-bok take on his second journey to Japan in 1696?
choices: A personal letter from the Joseon king
A map of the eight provinces of Joseon
A copy of Japan's sea-passage ban
questions.fact: On his second journey, An Yong-bok carried [[a map of the eight provinces of Joseon]].
questions.distractor: a personal letter from the Joseon king
questions.explain: The commoner fisherman unfolded a map of Joseon's territory before the shogunate's officials.
questions.tip: This pairs well with a comparison to the Murakami family documents.
questions.deep: An Yong-bok took a map of Joseon's eight provinces on his second journey in 1696. At the Hoki provincial office, he used it to point out Ulleungdo and Dokdo within Gangwon-do and argue that they were Joseon territory. The source presents this as a commoner using a national map to argue sovereignty before foreign officials.

wrong.0: He traveled privately and did not carry a royal diplomatic letter.
wrong.2: The source places the ban in January 1696; its chronology here needs review.
wrong.3: Ulleungdo was being kept uninhabited under Joseon's island policy.

questions.q: What is the average depth of the East Sea seabed plain from which Dokdo rises?
questions.fact: The East Sea seabed plain beneath Dokdo is about [[2,000 m]] deep on average.
questions.explain: Dokdo is the summit of a huge volcanic body rising from about 2,000 m below sea level.
questions.tip: Use the idea that there is much more below the surface to convey its scale.

questions.q: Where is Dokdo's only naturally flowing spring?
choices: At the summit of Usanbong on Dongdo
questions.fact: Dokdo's only natural spring is at [[Mulgol on northern Seodo]].
questions.distractor: the summit of Usanbong on Dongdo
questions.explain: The source links the freshwater supply to the question of whether an island can sustain human habitation.
questions.tip: More people chose Usanbong than the correct answer.
questions.deep: Mulgol is a cave-like spring below the northwestern coastal cliffs of Seodo (West Islet). This source gives its daily flow as about 1,000 liters and says Choi Jong-deok built 998 cement steps to reach it. The text links freshwater availability to the human-habitation criterion in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. The quantity and legal interpretation are retained for review, not independently verified here.

wrong.0: This is the docking area, not a freshwater source.
wrong.2: This summit attracted 37% of responses, more than the correct answer; it has no spring.
wrong.3: This places the spring on the opposite side.

questions.q: On what date was SCAPIN No. 677 issued?
questions.fact: SCAPIN No. 677 was issued on [[January 29, 1946]].
questions.explain: This was when the Allied command excluded Dokdo while defining Japan's postwar administrative scope.
questions.tip: Distinguish this date from other major dates in the period.

questions.q: What directly prompted President Syngman Rhee to declare the Peace Line in 1952?
choices: A sharp rise in Japanese fishing incursions
The planned abolition of the MacArthur Line
A UN recommendation to declare a maritime boundary
Japanese plans to build military facilities on Dokdo
questions.fact: The immediate context for the Peace Line was the planned [[abolition of the MacArthur Line]].
questions.explain: The government acted in advance of a change in the international political framework.
questions.tip: Many chose the plausible distraction about Japanese fishing boats.

questions.q: What kind of marine mammal was the gangchi that once lived on Dokdo?
questions.fact: The gangchi that once lived on Dokdo was a type of [[sea lion]].
questions.explain: The Dokdo sea lion was a sea mammal in the sea lion family. Tens of thousands once lived in the waters around Dokdo.
questions.tip: Rated easy, but only 32% got it right. Many confuse them with fur seals or seals.
questions.deep:
The gangchi was a sea lion. Sea lions and fur seals both belong to the eared-seal family and have visible ear flaps; true seals do not. Sea lions and fur seals can turn their hind flippers forward to move on land.

The supplied historical account describes large colonies around Dokdo in the early 1900s, followed by intensive hunting by Nakai Yozaburo and others. It dates the last sightings to the early 1970s. These population and last-sighting claims still require source-specific review.

wrong.0: True seals have no visible external ear flaps; the gangchi was a sea lion.
wrong.1: Sea otters belong to the weasel family, a completely different group.
wrong.2: Both are in the flipper-footed sea mammal group, but they are different species. This was the most common wrong answer.

questions.q: What name did Imperial Edict No. 41 of the Korean Empire use for Dokdo in 1900?
questions.fact: Imperial Edict No. 41 of 1900 called Dokdo [[Seokdo]].
questions.explain: Seokdo rendered the meaning of the local name 'stone island.' The dialect form Dokseom connects that name to today's Dokdo.
questions.tip: A question about historical names and language.
questions.deep: The Chinese-character rendering of the meaning of Dolseom, or 'stone island,' is Seokdo. In Gyeongsang and Jeolla dialects, dol could be pronounced dok, producing Dokseom; the name then settled into the character-based form Dokdo. The source presents this language history as the link between Seokdo in Imperial Edict No. 41 and present-day Dokdo.

wrong.0: This name was used from early Joseon, but is not the edict's term.
wrong.1: This is the name An Yong-bok used in Japan.
wrong.2: This nickname refers to the abundance of sea lions.

questions.q: What is the name of the Tokyo exhibition facility Japan opened to promote its territorial claims?
choices: National Museum of Territory and Sovereignty
questions.fact: The Tokyo facility promoting Japan's territorial claims is the [[National Museum of Territory and Sovereignty]].
questions.explain: The source describes it as a state-funded center for territorial-revisionist publicity, originally near Hibiya Park.
questions.tip: Remember the facility's exact name.
questions.deep: The museum opened in the basement of the Municipal Research Building near Tokyo's Hibiya Park in 2018, moved to a larger site in Toranomon in 2020, and expanded again in 2025. The source interprets the broad phrase 'territory and sovereignty' as a way to group Japan's claims concerning Dokdo, the Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands and the Kuril Islands into a national territorial agenda.

wrong.0: This sounds plausible but is not the facility's actual name.
wrong.2: This is not the facility's name.
wrong.3: This confuses it with a separate facility in Shimane Prefecture.

questions.q: Which Joseon official is identified in the source as leaving a detailed observation of Dokdo in a 1711 record?
questions.fact: The Samcheok commander identified in the source's 1711 Ulleungdo inspection record is [[Jang Han-sang]].
questions.explain: The record describes an island visible to the southeast, smaller than one-third of Ulleungdo.
questions.tip: Only 18% answered correctly; the famous An Yong-bok drew many responses.
questions.deep: Jang Han-sang inspected Ulleungdo as Samcheok commander in 1694. The supplied text attributes to a 1711 record his description of an island to the southeast, less than one-third the size of Ulleungdo and more than 300 ri away. It interprets the observation as evidence of Joseon's knowledge of Dokdo. The differing inspection and record dates need editorial review.

wrong.0: An early-Joseon island official, about 300 years earlier.
wrong.1: He observed Sambongdo under King Seongjong, about 200 years earlier.
wrong.2: He was a contemporary, but a fisherman rather than this government official.

questions.q: Where is Dokdo's helicopter landing pad?
choices: In the channel between the two islets
On the upper part of Dongdo
questions.fact: Dokdo's helicopter landing pad is [[on the upper part of Dongdo]].
questions.explain: It is a key transport facility on the ridge near the guard post and lighthouse.
questions.tip: It connects the island with regular official transport and administration.
questions.deep: The source describes a roughly 400 m² landing pad in front of the guards' quarters on upper Dongdo (East Islet). The lighthouse, dock, desalination equipment and satellite antenna are also on Dongdo, making it the administrative and guard center. Seodo (West Islet) has the natural spring called Mulgol.

wrong.0: The steep slope is unsuitable for this landing pad.
wrong.1: This is open water.
wrong.3: Mulgol is a water source, not an aviation facility.

questions.q: According to the source, what mainly causes seaweed loss and barren seabeds around Dokdo?
choices: Rising water temperatures and more starfish
Illegal seaweed gathering by Japanese boats
questions.fact: The source identifies [[rising water temperatures and more starfish]] as the main cause of the barren-seabed phenomenon.
questions.explain: This is described as 'marine desertification,' in which seaweed forests are lost and the seabed becomes pale and barren.
questions.tip: An environmental question about warming; the organism identified in the source needs review.

questions.q: What international-law argument did Japan invoke when incorporating Dokdo in 1905?
questions.fact: Japan's stated basis for the 1905 incorporation was [[occupation of terra nullius]].
questions.explain: The source challenges the ownerless-land argument using Imperial Edict No. 41 of 1900 and Japan's own Dajokan Directive of 1877.
questions.tip: A central question in the legal argument.

questions.q: In what year and under what number was Dokdo designated a Natural Monument?
questions.fact: Dokdo was designated Natural Monument No. 336 in [[1982]].
questions.explain: This marked legal protection of Dokdo's ecology as well as recognition of its territorial importance.
questions.tip: Remember both the year and the heritage number.
questions.deep: The supplied account dates the initial designation to November 1982 and says that it was renamed 'Dokdo Natural Reserve' in 1999, extending protection to the whole island group. It presents legal conservation measures as an exercise of jurisdiction. The wording and date of the original designation should be checked against the heritage record.

wrong.0: This is not the correct year-number combination.
wrong.1: This is not the correct year-number combination.
wrong.2: This may be confused with the 1999 change of name.

questions.q: What ocean process brings deep-water nutrients upward around Dokdo?
questions.fact: The rise of nutrients from deep water to the surface is called [[upwelling]].
questions.explain: The source describes the meeting of the North Korea Cold Current and East Korea Warm Current as drawing nutrients upward.
questions.tip: This connects Dokdo's rich fishing grounds with ocean science.

questions.q: Which seafood did Choi Jong-deok, Dokdo's first civilian resident, mainly gather on Seodo (West Islet)?
questions.fact: On Seodo (West Islet), Choi Jong-deok mainly gathered [[abalone and turban snails]].
questions.explain: He settled alone on Seodo (West Islet) in 1965. His hard work to earn a living there showed Korea's control in action.
questions.tip: This is where the story of Dokdo's civilian pioneers begins.

questions.q: What old island name appears in Kim Ja-ju's drawing presented to King Seongjong of Joseon?
questions.fact: The old island name in Kim Ja-ju's drawing for King Seongjong was [[Sambongdo]].
questions.explain: He sailed from Hamgyeong-do, saw an island with three peaks, and presented a detailed drawing.
questions.tip: A question linking historical observations and island landforms.

questions.q: Which seaweed is described in the source as characteristic of the coasts of Ulleungdo and Dokdo?
questions.fact: The seaweed described as forming large forests off Ulleungdo and Dokdo is [[daehwang]].
questions.explain: The supplied text describes daehwang as a rare seaweed restricted to the clean waters of Ulleungdo and Dokdo; that geographic restriction needs review.
questions.tip: A science question about conserving marine ecosystems.

questions.q: What did the Joseon court do after An Yong-bok's two journeys to Japan?
questions.fact: After An Yong-bok's return, the Joseon court's action was [[exile]].
questions.explain: He was punished for crossing the border without authority. The source connects his activities with the Edo shogunate's passage ban.
questions.tip: The court punished him, but history remembers his courage.

questions.q: How did the Dokdo Volunteer Garrison obtain money for weapons?
choices: Free supplies from the US military
Profits from squid trading, then purchases in Daegu
Weapons retained from the Korean War
questions.fact: Commander Hong Sun-chil raised money to buy weapons by trading [[squid]].
questions.explain: He bought squid on Ulleungdo, resold it in Busan to double the funds, and obtained M1 rifles and a mortar on the Daegu black market.
questions.tip: A striking example of resourcefulness in a civilian defense effort.

questions.q: How did Uldo County Magistrate Sim Heung-taek learn of Japan's incorporation of Dokdo in 1906?
choices: An official notice from the Korean Empire's Foreign Ministry
A visiting Shimane Prefecture inspection team told him
Fishermen reported finding a Japanese marker
He read an announcement in Japan's national gazette
questions.fact: Sim Heung-taek learned of the incorporation from [[a Shimane Prefecture inspection team]] visiting Uldo County.
questions.distractor: an official from the Korean Empire's Foreign Ministry
questions.explain: Shocked, he urgently reported that Dokdo, belonging to his county, had been taken by Japan.
questions.tip: Keep the historical sequence clear.
questions.deep: A Shimane Prefecture inspection team visited Ulleungdo on March 28, 1906, and said that Dokdo had become Japanese territory. The following day, Sim Heung-taek sent an urgent report to the governor of Gangwon-do, identifying Dokdo as belonging to his county. That description is central to the source's argument that Dokdo was already under Uldo County's jurisdiction.

wrong.0: Japan had not sent such a notice, so the government had not received one.
wrong.2: The marker installation belongs to a later event.
wrong.3: There was no such announcement in the national gazette.

questions.q: When was the Dokdo sea lion last reported seen, according to the source?
questions.fact: The last reported sightings of the Dokdo sea lion were in [[the early 1970s]].
questions.explain: Once numbering in the tens of thousands, the sea lions declined through intensive Japanese commercial hunting and disappeared in the early 1970s.
questions.tip: A tragedy in ecological history.
questions.deep: Tens of thousands of sea lions lived on Dokdo in the early 1900s. Nakai Yozaburo sought exclusive hunting rights when petitioning for the island's incorporation in 1905. The source says more than 14,000 were caught between 1904 and 1913, the population collapsed, and sightings ended in the early 1970s.

wrong.0: This confuses the incorporation year with extinction; many still lived there then.
wrong.1: Small numbers were still observed during the Pacific War period.
wrong.2: Later sightings are recorded.

questions.q: Which island did the Japanese name 'Takeshima,' now used by Japan for Dokdo, originally refer to?
questions.fact: Before the Meiji era, the Japanese name 'Takeshima' referred to [[Ulleungdo]].
questions.explain: Before the Meiji Restoration, Japan called Ulleungdo 'Takeshima' and Dokdo 'Matsushima.' The source describes the name being reassigned in 1905.
questions.tip: This question highlights how historical names changed their referents.
questions.deep: Before the Meiji Restoration, Japanese usage called Ulleungdo 'Takeshima' and Dokdo 'Matsushima.' Name confusion followed Western mapping after a French vessel recorded Dokdo in 1849. When Japan incorporated Dokdo in 1905, it applied to Dokdo the name that had formerly denoted Ulleungdo.

wrong.0: These Japanese islands are not the subject of this name transfer.
wrong.1: This is a separate island between Korea and Japan.
wrong.3: These islands are involved in a separate dispute and are unrelated to this naming history.

questions.q: How did the Dokdo Volunteer Garrison deter approaching Japanese aircraft?
questions.fact: The Dokdo Volunteer Garrison painted [[logs]] black to make them look like cannons.
questions.explain: The story illustrates Commander Hong Sun-chil's and the volunteers' ingenuity when weapons were scarce.
questions.tip: A memorable example of resourcefulness.

questions.q: How did President Roh Moo-hyun frame the Dokdo issue in his 2006 special address?
choices: A matter of addressing the history of Japanese aggression
A task for joint Korean-Japanese management
questions.fact: Roh Moo-hyun described Dokdo as a matter of [[addressing the history of Japanese aggression]].
questions.explain: He made the statement in response to Japan's planned maritime survey near Dokdo.
questions.tip: The source describes him working through the night on the address.

questions.q: When did the Korean Empire learn of Japan's 1905 incorporation of Dokdo?
questions.fact: The Korean Empire learned of the 1905 incorporation only [[a year later, in March 1906]].
questions.explain: The source treats the year-long absence of notification as evidence against the legitimacy of the incorporation.
questions.tip: The delay is the key point of this question.
questions.deep: Shimane Prefecture issued Notice No. 40 in February 1905 without notifying the Korean Empire. Sim Heung-taek first learned of it when a visiting Shimane inspection team mentioned it orally in March of the following year. The source argues that the failure to notify an interested state undermined Japan's claimed legal procedure.

wrong.0: The source says there was no immediate notification.
wrong.1: No notification is recorded at this time either.
wrong.3: It became known in March 1906 through a visit, not a formal diplomatic document.

questions.q: How often do Dokdo's guards change teams?
questions.fact: Dokdo's guard teams change about every [[2 months]].
questions.explain: Even with little space and rough waves, the guards keep a tight watch 24 hours a day.
questions.tip: Give the guards credit for their hard work in tough conditions.
questions.deep: About 40 members of the Dokdo Guard serve under the Gyeongsangbuk-do Provincial Police Agency. They switch teams every 2 months. The key point is that police, not soldiers, guard Dokdo. An area in dispute would have soldiers. But Dokdo is an ordinary part of the Republic of Korea where the police keep order, so police are stationed there.

wrong.0: You may be thinking of how often supply boats run.
wrong.2: That is too long, given how hard it is to work cut off from other people.
wrong.3: That is six times the actual period.

questions.q: What did Choi Jong-deok build to reach Mulgol, Seodo's water source?
choices: A rope ladder on the cliff
questions.fact: Choi Jong-deok built [[998]] cement steps to reach Mulgol.
questions.explain: He carried sacks of cement himself and made a path on the cliff.
questions.tip: A moving story about the effort behind everyday life on Dokdo.

questions.q: What happens if you send a letter to Dokdo?
choices: It is delivered; the mailbox has regular pickups
It is delivered only as far as Ulleungdo
It is blocked because Dokdo is a military area
It is sent back because Dokdo has no postal code
questions.fact: Dokdo has a mailbox, and letters [[are delivered]].
questions.explain: Dokdo's official postal code and regular pickups by mail carriers show Korea's public services at work.
questions.tip: The best quiz for showing sovereignty in everyday life.

questions.q: According to this source, when did Japan begin the school teaching about Dokdo described here?
questions.fact: The source dates the start of the Dokdo curriculum campaign to [[2008]].
questions.explain: This is the year given for the explanatory guidance accompanying Japan's curriculum standards.
questions.tip: The school level and chronology need editorial review.
questions.deep: The supplied text traces the change to explanatory guidance for junior-high curricula in 2008, expansion to elementary schools in 2014, and broader textbook coverage in 2017. Its original question instead specifies elementary schools, and its age calculation for pupils is inconsistent. Those discrepancies are documented in the review notes rather than resolved as new historical claims.

wrong.0: The source says textbooks rarely included such statements then.
wrong.1: This is the year Shimane introduced its 'Takeshima Day' designation concerning Dokdo.
wrong.2: The source cites prewar maps that instead placed Dokdo with Joseon.

questions.q: According to the source's 2025 figure, how many Japanese citizens registered their family domicile on Dokdo under Japan's name for it?
questions.fact: The source gives [[112]] Japanese domicile registrations on Dokdo as of 2025.
questions.explain: The source contrasts this small number with campaigns by Japanese right-wing groups.
questions.tip: Compare it with the source's separate honorary-resident certificate figure.

questions.q: When did LTE mobile service first open on Dokdo?
questions.fact: LTE service on Dokdo opened on [[Liberation Day in 2013]].
questions.explain: The source emphasizes that service began on Liberation Day as part of Korea's communications infrastructure on the island.
questions.tip: Many confuse Dokdo Day with Liberation Day.
questions.deep: LTE service opened on August 15, 2013. Building and maintaining a commercial mobile network more than 200 km from the mainland demonstrates continuing infrastructure management. The source pairs it with the satellite internet service introduced in 2000 as an example of modern administration.

wrong.0: This confuses Dokdo Day with the actual opening date.
wrong.1: This is not the recorded date.
wrong.3: This is not the recorded date.

questions.q: What punishment did Hachiemon receive after violating the ban on travel to Ulleungdo, in the event dated 1837 by the source?
questions.fact: The source gives Hachiemon's punishment as [[execution]].
questions.explain: It interprets the shogunate's severe punishment as reflecting its recognition of the islands as Joseon territory.
questions.tip: A question based on a historical legal case.

questions.q: Which is the oldest document Japan cites in support of its Dokdo claim, according to the source?
questions.fact: The oldest document identified here is the [[Onshu Shicho Goki]] of 1667.
questions.explain: The text points out that this document places Japan's northwestern limit at the Oki Islands, outside which Dokdo lies.
questions.tip: Compare its date with Isabu's expedition in 512: more than 1,100 years apart.

questions.q: What is the largest vessel class that Dokdo's docking facility can accommodate?
questions.fact: Dokdo's docking facility can accommodate vessels up to the [[500-ton class]].
questions.explain: The movement of people and supplies through the facility is an example of continuing administration.
questions.tip: The larger ship classes are plausible distractions.
questions.deep: An 80 m docking facility was completed on Dongdo (East Islet) in November 1997. Before that, even moderately rough water made landing difficult. The source links the facility to the 2005 opening for public visits and reports a cumulative 3.6 million visitors.

wrong.0: This underestimates the facility's capacity.
wrong.2: This exceeds the stated capacity.
wrong.3: This large passenger-ship class exceeds the facility's stated capacity.

questions.q: How does Dokdo's evergreen spindle grow differently from the same species inland?
choices: Its branches spread close to the ground in strong sea winds
It grows faster by absorbing seawater
It reproduces only by roots and never flowers
It sheds leaves in winter to conserve water
questions.fact: Strong sea winds make Dokdo's evergreen spindle spread [[close to the ground]].
questions.explain: The tree, more than 100 years old, is designated Natural Monument No. 538.
questions.tip: Its shape offers a memorable image of endurance.

questions.q: What did SCAPIN No. 1033 prohibit around Dokdo?
choices: It ordered Dokdo returned to Korea
It established a US military base
It barred Japanese vessels within 12 nautical miles
It placed Dokdo under UN trusteeship
questions.fact: SCAPIN No. 1033 barred Japanese vessels from approaching within [[12 nautical miles]] of Dokdo.
questions.explain: SCAPIN No. 677 concerned administrative separation; No. 1033 restricted physical access by Japanese vessels.
questions.tip: Remember the different roles of the two directives.

questions.q: What was the purpose of Joseon's policy of keeping Ulleungdo and Dokdo uninhabited?
choices: Preparing to transfer it to Japan
questions.fact: The island-evacuation policy aimed at [[protecting residents from pirate raids]].
questions.explain: Evacuating residents for protection is different from abandoning territory. Joseon continued to send inspection officials.
questions.tip: This question had the highest correct-answer rate and works well as a story.

questions.q: In what year did Japan first open the National Museum of Territory and Sovereignty in Tokyo?
questions.fact: The National Museum of Territory and Sovereignty first opened in Tokyo in [[2018]].
questions.explain: It first opened near Hibiya Park in 2018, relocated to a larger site in 2020 and expanded again in 2025.
questions.tip: Keep the initial opening distinct from later expansion.
questions.deep: The museum opened in January 2018 in about 100 m² in the basement of the Municipal Research Building near Hibiya Park. It moved to Toranomon in 2020, expanding about sevenfold, then expanded again in 2025. The source interprets the three stages in seven years as a coordinated national-budget project rather than a private or merely local initiative.

wrong.1: The facility had not yet opened.
wrong.2: The facility had not yet opened.
wrong.3: This was the relocation and expansion year, not the first opening.

questions.q: How did Korea's Foreign Ministry respond to the museum's additional expansion in 2025?
choices: Submitted a formal protest to the UN
Summoned Japan's deputy chief of mission and urged closure
Announced a break in diplomatic relations
questions.fact: In 2025, Korea's Foreign Ministry [[summoned Japan's deputy chief of mission]] and urged the facility's closure.
questions.distractor: submitted a protest to the UN
questions.explain: The source says the ministry summoned Deputy Chief of Mission Matsuo and strongly protested.
questions.tip: The source identifies this as a diplomatic issue from November 2025.

questions.q: Which document is identified by the source as making Japan's Dokdo textbook policy binding in practice?
choices: A white paper on Japan's Dokdo claim
Explanatory notes to the curriculum standards
questions.fact: The document identified here is the [[explanatory notes to the curriculum standards]].
questions.distractor: white paper on Japan's Dokdo claim
questions.explain: The source describes these notes as requiring textbooks to repeat Japan's claims about Dokdo from 2008.
questions.tip: A difficult question about law and the education system.
questions.deep: The source distinguishes the curriculum framework from the accompanying explanatory notes, which it describes as the practical basis for textbook approval. It says the 2008 junior-high social-studies notes required presentation of Dokdo as Japanese territory, leaving publishers unable to secure approval otherwise. It views this as a shift from individual publishers' choices to state direction.

wrong.0: A prefectural ordinance does not govern all national textbooks.
wrong.1: This concerns a museum that opened in 2018.
wrong.2: Foreign Ministry publicity is not the curriculum document asked for.

questions.q: According to the source's 2026 figure, roughly how many Dokdo honorary-resident certificates had been issued?
questions.fact: The source gives a cumulative total of about [[150,000]] honorary-resident certificates as of 2026.
questions.explain: The source contrasts 150,000 expressions of public interest with its statement that there were no ordinary civilian residents at that point.
questions.tip: Compare with the separate Japanese family-domicile figure, keeping the two systems distinct.
questions.deep: The source describes Ulleung County's honorary-resident scheme as beginning in 2005. It is a symbolic registration of interest, not actual residence, and the text reports 150,000 applicants. It compares this with 112 Japanese family-domicile registrations. The dates and totals are retained as source figures, not updated statistics.

wrong.0: The source associates this with the scheme's early scale.
wrong.1: The source associates this with the early 2010s.
wrong.3: This overestimates the stated total.

questions.q: Which well-known plant grows purple flowers in cracks in Dokdo's rocks?
questions.fact: The [[seashore aster]] is a well-known plant that grows purple flowers in cracks in Dokdo's rocks.
questions.explain: Also called 'sea chrysanthemum,' the seashore aster takes root in cracks on bare seaside cliffs. Its purple flowers color Dokdo from summer to fall.
questions.tip: Rated easy, but only about half get it right. A nice chance to connect over nature.

questions.q: What name for Dokdo appears in Japan's 1870 report on relations with Joseon?
choices: Takeshima (the name Japan now applies to Dokdo)
questions.fact: The 1870 report called Dokdo [[Matsushima (Songdo)]].
questions.explain: The Japanese Foreign Ministry's report included a section about how the islands became associated with Joseon, which the source treats as recognition of Joseon's territory.
questions.tip: A difficult historical-name question with a low correct-answer rate.
questions.deep: The report was submitted to the Meiji Foreign Ministry after an investigation of conditions in Joseon. A section addressed how Ulleungdo and Dokdo became dependencies of Joseon, using the contemporary Japanese names Takeshima and Matsushima. The source emphasizes that this Japanese government record predates the claimed incorporation of 1905 by 35 years.

wrong.1: At that time this Japanese name referred to Ulleungdo.
wrong.2: This Western name came from a French whaling ship in 1849.
wrong.3: This is a name from Joseon records.

questions.q: When is Dokdo Day?
questions.fact: Dokdo Day is [[October 25]].
questions.explain: Dokdo Day marks October 25, 1900. On that day, Emperor Gojong issued Imperial Edict No. 41 of the Korean Empire, officially making Dokdo part of Ulleung County.
questions.tip: A symbolic question for the 100th-episode special. Keep it light.

questions.q: Which sea is Dokdo in?
questions.fact: Dokdo is Korean land in [[the East Sea]].
questions.explain: Dokdo is the island farthest east in Korea. It is the first place in Korea to see the sunrise.
questions.tip: Start here: this is the most basic question.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which bird is seen most often on Dokdo?
questions.fact: The bird seen most often on Dokdo is the [[black-tailed gull]].
questions.explain: The black-tailed gull gets its Korean name from its cat-like cry. It is known as an old-timer on Dokdo.
questions.tip: Tell kids about its cat-like cry. They love it.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How many large islands make up Dokdo?
questions.fact: Dokdo is made up of [[2]] large islands and smaller rocky islands.
questions.explain: The two large islands are Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet). Small rocky islands lie around them.
questions.tip: Students learn the names Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet) in the next grade.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What shines a light out to sea from Dokdo at night?
questions.fact: Dokdo has a [[lighthouse]] that lights up the sea at night.
questions.explain: Dokdo Lighthouse stands on top of Dongdo (East Islet). It helps passing ships find their way.
questions.tip: The lighthouse story ties in with the light-up map.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What do you ride to get to Dokdo?
questions.fact: People travel to Dokdo by [[boat]].
questions.explain: You take a boat from Ulleungdo. On days with high waves, boats may not sail, so visitors may have to turn back.
questions.tip: A natural way to explain why sailings get canceled.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What are the names of Dokdo's two large islands?
questions.fact: Dokdo's two large islands are [[Dongdo (East Islet) and Seodo (West Islet)]].
questions.explain: Dongdo (East Islet) gets its name from being on the east side. Seodo (West Islet) gets its name from being on the west side. The sea between them is very shallow.
questions.tip: Their names match their directions, so they're easy to remember.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which island is Dokdo's lighthouse on?
questions.fact: Dokdo's lighthouse is on [[Dongdo (East Islet)]].
questions.explain: The guards' rooms are also on Dongdo (East Islet). So are the helicopter landing pad and the boat dock.
questions.tip: People come and go on Dongdo (East Islet); Seodo (West Islet) has a water source.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which is the only bird that lives on Dokdo all year?
questions.fact: The only bird that lives on Dokdo all year is the [[sparrow]].
questions.explain: Other birds come and go with the seasons. Sparrows stay on Dokdo all year.
questions.tip: People are often surprised that sparrows live on Dokdo, too.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which province is Dokdo part of?
questions.fact: Dokdo is part of Ulleung County in [[Gyeongsangbuk-do]].
questions.explain: Dokdo's address is Dokdo-ri, Ulleung-eup, Ulleung-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do.
questions.tip: Having a Korean address is itself evidence that Dokdo is Korean territory.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How was Dokdo formed?
questions.fact: Dokdo was formed when [[an underwater volcano rose up]].
questions.explain: Dokdo is the top of a huge volcano that rose from 2,000 m below the sea.
questions.tip: It's the older sibling: Dokdo formed before Ulleungdo.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: When do black-tailed gulls lay eggs and raise chicks on Dokdo?
questions.fact: Black-tailed gulls raise their chicks on Dokdo [[from spring to summer]].
questions.explain: From late March to July, Dokdo becomes a giant nursery for black-tailed gulls.
questions.tip: Photos from this season show Dokdo blanketed in white birds.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: What is the name of the highest peak on Dokdo's Dongdo (East Islet)?
questions.fact: The highest peak on Dokdo's Dongdo (East Islet) is [[Usanbong]].
questions.explain: Daehanbong is the highest point on Seodo (West Islet). Usanbong is the highest point on Dongdo (East Islet).
questions.tip: The name comes from Usando, an old name for Dokdo.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How high is Dokdo's highest point?
questions.fact: Dokdo's highest point is Daehanbong on Seodo (West Islet), at about [[168 m]].
questions.explain: Usanbong on Dongdo (East Islet) is 98.6 m high, while Daehanbong on Seodo (West Islet) is 168.5 m. Seodo is much higher and steeper.
questions.tip: Think of roughly a 50-story apartment building.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How far can Dokdo Lighthouse's light reach?
questions.fact: Dokdo Lighthouse's light reaches about [[25 nautical miles]].
questions.explain: Its light can be seen from about 46 km away at sea.
questions.tip: In the dark East Sea, the light marks the island.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: How do people on Dokdo obtain drinking water?
choices: By turning seawater into fresh water
By digging deep into the ground
questions.fact: Dokdo obtains water using equipment that [[turns seawater into fresh water]].
questions.explain: The source gives production as 27 tons a day. Seodo (West Islet) also has a natural spring called Mulgol.
questions.tip: This connects daily life with the question of an island's ability to sustain habitation.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which bird of prey raises its young on the high cliffs of Seodo (West Islet)?
questions.fact: [[Falcons]] raise their young on the cliffs of Seodo (West Islet).
questions.explain: Cliffs that are difficult for people to climb provide safe nesting places for falcons.
questions.tip: Contrast Dongdo's facilities with Seodo's birds and trees.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: In which year was Dokdo Lighthouse first lit?
questions.fact: Dokdo Lighthouse was first lit in [[1954]].
questions.explain: The lighthouse first shone in August 1954, nine years after Korea's liberation.
questions.tip: This was during the Dokdo Volunteer Garrison's activity.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which is Dokdo's administrative address?
questions.fact: Dokdo's address is [[Dokdo-ri, Ulleung-eup, Ulleung-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do]].
questions.explain: It has a formal address, including lot numbers. Letters are delivered using postal code 40240.
questions.tip: Connect the administrative address, postal code and road names.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: In which year was Dokdo's docking facility built?
questions.fact: Dokdo's docking facility was built in [[1997]].
questions.explain: The 80 m facility on Dongdo (East Islet) enabled vessels of up to the 500-ton class to dock.
questions.tip: The facility helped make public visits possible.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: About how many bird species are reported in the source as observed on Dokdo?
questions.fact: The source reports about [[80]] bird species observed on Dokdo.
questions.explain: Despite its small size, Dokdo lies on a migration route. The text reports more than 15,000 visiting birds each year.
questions.tip: A small island can support a large ecological story.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: In which year was an internet satellite antenna installed on Dokdo?
questions.fact: An internet satellite antenna was installed on Dokdo in [[2000]].
questions.explain: Satellite internet in 2000 and LTE in 2013 connected the island more closely with the mainland.
questions.tip: A timeline of infrastructure and modern administration.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q: Which tree on Dokdo, more than 100 years old, became a Natural Monument?
questions.fact: Dokdo's tree older than 100 years and designated a Natural Monument is an [[evergreen spindle]].
questions.explain: Strong sea winds keep it close to the ground, but it has endured for more than a century.
questions.tip: Its endurance makes a memorable image.
questions.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), official Dokdo website; Northeast Asian History Foundation (NAHF)

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Area: Dongdo (East Islet) 73,297 m²; Seodo (West Islet) 88,740 m²; smaller islands 25,517 m²; total 187,554 m².

Subtract the smaller islands from the total. What is the combined area of the two main islets?
questions.fact: Subtracting 25,517 m² from 187,554 m² gives a combined main-islet area of [[162,037 m²]].
questions.explain: Subtract the smaller islands: 187,554 - 25,517 = 162,037 m². Adding the two main islets gives the same result.
questions.deep: The total consists of Dongdo, Seodo and the smaller islands. First distinguish the whole from the part being asked for. This is an aggregation of the supplied land areas; it does not add the sea shown on a map or the channel between the islets.

wrong.1: This total still includes the smaller islands.
wrong.2: This is the difference between the two main-islet areas.
wrong.3: This is the area to be excluded.

questions.src: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo Overview (2024-12-31), area/height/coastline table; https://gb.go.kr/Main/marinefishery/page.do?LARGE_CODE=1100&MEDIUM_CODE=20&mnu_order=2&mnu_uid=15954 ; Cross-reference: KIOST, Dokdo Integrated Information System, Size; https://www.dokdo.re.kr/home/cms/cmsCont.do?cntnts_sn=64

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Dongdo (East Islet): 73,297 m². Total Dokdo land area: 187,554 m².

What percentage of the total is Dongdo, rounded to one decimal place for a pie chart?
questions.fact: Dongdo's 73,297 m² as a percentage of 187,554 m² rounds to [[39.1%]].
questions.explain: Divide Dongdo's area by the total and multiply by 100. About 39.08% rounds to 39.1%.
questions.deep: Define the whole before calculating a percentage. The denominator here is all of Dokdo, including the smaller islands, not just the two main islets. Keep sufficient decimal places during the division and round only at the end.

wrong.0: This is Seodo's share of the total.
wrong.2: This is the smaller islands' share.
wrong.3: This combines Dongdo and Seodo.

questions.src: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo Overview (2024-12-31), area/height/coastline table; https://gb.go.kr/Main/marinefishery/page.do?LARGE_CODE=1100&MEDIUM_CODE=20&mnu_order=2&mnu_uid=15954 ; Cross-reference: KIOST, Dokdo Integrated Information System, Size; https://www.dokdo.re.kr/home/cms/cmsCont.do?cntnts_sn=64

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Heights: Dongdo (East Islet) 98.6 m, Seodo (West Islet) 168.5 m. Coastlines: Dongdo 2.8 km, Seodo 2.6 km.

What is the difference between the two stated heights?
questions.fact: The difference between 168.5 m and 98.6 m is [[69.9 m]].
questions.explain: Use the height measurements in meters: 168.5 - 98.6 = 69.9 m. Do not use the coastline figures in kilometers.
questions.deep: Area, height and coastline length may appear in one table, but they are not interchangeable. Select the same measurement for both islets before finding a difference. This result is not the full height of a particular cliff or the depth of the channel.

wrong.0: This adds the heights instead of subtracting them.
wrong.1: This misuses the coastline difference as a height difference.
wrong.3: The result must remain in meters, not kilometers.

questions.src: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo Overview (2024-12-31), area/height/coastline table; https://gb.go.kr/Main/marinefishery/page.do?LARGE_CODE=1100&MEDIUM_CODE=20&mnu_order=2&mnu_uid=15954 ; Cross-reference: KIOST, Dokdo Integrated Information System, Size; https://www.dokdo.re.kr/home/cms/cmsCont.do?cntnts_sn=64

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Dongdo (East Islet): 73,297 m², coastline 2.8 km. Seodo (West Islet): 88,740 m², coastline 2.6 km.

Compare coastline per 10,000 m² using (coastline in m / area in m²) x 10,000. Which result is correct?
questions.fact: Comparing coastline per 10,000 m² gives [[a longer value for Dongdo]].
questions.explain: Convert coastline lengths to meters. Dongdo has about 382 m per 10,000 m², compared with about 293 m for Seodo.
questions.deep: Using the same area denominator makes differently sized islands comparable. This is only an indicator calculated from the table. It cannot by itself determine the difficulty of field surveys or the ecological value of either islet.

wrong.0: A larger area does not by itself mean a longer coastline per unit area.
wrong.1: The results differ: about 382 m versus 293 m.
wrong.2: After converting km to m, the supplied formula allows comparison.

questions.src: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo Overview (2024-12-31), area/height/coastline table; https://gb.go.kr/Main/marinefishery/page.do?LARGE_CODE=1100&MEDIUM_CODE=20&mnu_order=2&mnu_uid=15954 ; Cross-reference: KIOST, Dokdo Integrated Information System, Size; https://www.dokdo.re.kr/home/cms/cmsCont.do?cntnts_sn=64

questions.q:
[Source: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo general information, December 31, 2024]
Dongdo (East Islet): 73,297 m², coastline 2.8 km. Seodo (West Islet): 88,740 m², coastline 2.6 km.

A caption says, "Of these two islets, the one with the larger area also has the longer coastline." How does the table test that claim?
questions.fact: Seodo's larger area but shorter coastline provides a [[counterexample]] to the claim.
questions.explain: Seodo has the larger area but a 2.6 km coastline, shorter than Dongdo's 2.8 km. The claim does not fit the table.
questions.deep: Do not assume two different measurements always move in the same direction. Check the objects and conditions in a claim, then look for a case that meets those conditions but contradicts its conclusion. That is the counterexample sought here.

wrong.1: Seodo is larger in area but shorter in coastline.
wrong.2: Height is not the coastline measure in the claim.
wrong.3: The coastlines are 2.8 km and 2.6 km, not equal.

questions.src: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Dokdo Overview (2024-12-31), area/height/coastline table; https://gb.go.kr/Main/marinefishery/page.do?LARGE_CODE=1100&MEDIUM_CODE=20&mnu_order=2&mnu_uid=15954 ; Cross-reference: KIOST, Dokdo Integrated Information System, Size; https://www.dokdo.re.kr/home/cms/cmsCont.do?cntnts_sn=64

questions.q:
[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 1 renames Ulleungdo as Uldo and replaces the island superintendent with a county magistrate.

Update two fields in a hypothetical pre-reform register: "Administrative name: Ulleungdo / Official title: island superintendent." Which pair fits Article 1?
questions.fact: Applying both changes in Article 1 gives [[Uldo / county magistrate]].
questions.explain: Article 1 changes both the administrative name and the official title. Both register fields must be updated.
questions.deep: This asks you to apply a document's provisions to record fields. Changing only the name or only the title implements only part of the reform. The register is a teaching example, not a quotation from a surviving historical register.

wrong.0: Both fields retain their old forms.
wrong.2: Only the administrative name has changed.
wrong.3: Only the official title has changed.

questions.q:
[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 2 places the county office in Taeha-dong and gives it jurisdiction over all Ulleungdo, Jukdo and Seokdo.

A draft says "Office location: all Ulleungdo, Jukdo and Seokdo / Jurisdiction: Taeha-dong." How should it be corrected?
questions.fact: The draft reverses office location and jurisdiction, so the correction is [[to exchange the two fields' contents]].
questions.distractor: to change only the office location
blankDistractors: to change only the office location
questions.explain: The location and the area of jurisdiction have been reversed. Exchanging them brings both fields into line with Article 2.
questions.deep: Where an institution is located and the area it administers are different kinds of information. Mixing them merely because both contain place names changes the meaning of an administrative record. Both fields need checking, not just one.

wrong.0: The jurisdiction would still incorrectly be Taeha-dong.
wrong.1: The office location would still be a list of islands.
wrong.3: The office location and jurisdiction are reversed.

questions.q:
[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 4 gives priority to taxes collected on the island to fund initial expenses.

[Hypothetical budget] Expenses are 100 nyang, and 40 nyang of island taxes are available. After applying that 40 nyang, what shortfall remains?
questions.fact: In the hypothetical budget, 100 nyang of expenses minus 40 nyang of revenue leaves [[60 nyang]].
questions.explain: Subtract the available funding from the need: 100 - 40 = 60 nyang. These amounts are hypothetical, not historical statistics.
questions.deep: Article 4 states a funding priority; it does not supply the budget amounts used in this exercise. Distinguish the documented funding principle from the author's calculation assumptions. This extract does not tell us how much was obtained from other sources.

wrong.0: This is the funding already applied, not the shortfall.
wrong.1: This is the original total need.
wrong.2: Adding need and revenue does not give a shortfall.

questions.q:
[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 5 provides for later supplementation of incomplete rules. Article 6 makes the edict effective from promulgation.

An editor writes, "The edict does not take effect until every incomplete rule is supplemented." What correction applies both articles?
choices: Delay commencement until all rules are complete
Delete supplementation because the edict is already effective
questions.fact: Reading Articles 5 and 6 together requires [[separating commencement from supplementation]].
questions.distractor: delaying commencement until supplementation is complete
blankDistractors: delaying commencement until supplementation is complete
Treat enforcement and later revision as identical
questions.explain: Article 5 concerns later additions, while Article 6 fixes commencement. Neither says that unfinished details postpone commencement.
questions.deep: Identify what each provision governs. An immediate effective date and later additions to detailed rules can coexist. Adding a postponement condition that the text does not contain changes the source.

wrong.1: This changes Article 6's effective-date rule.
wrong.2: Immediate effect and later supplementation can coexist.
wrong.3: The provision directly governing commencement cannot be ignored.

[Source: Imperial Edict No. 41; summary of the Foreign Ministry translation]
Article 1: Gangwon-do affiliation and magistrate title. Article 2: Taeha-dong office and jurisdiction over Ulleungdo, Jukdo and Seokdo. Article 4: initial expenses funded first from taxes.

Match A=province and title, B=office location and jurisdiction, C=initial funding. Which articles match A, B and C in order?
questions.fact: The article order for organization, location/jurisdiction and initial funding is [[1 / 2 / 4]].
questions.explain: Match each check to its topic: Article 1 for organization, Article 2 for location and jurisdiction, and Article 4 for initial funding.
questions.deep: Citing a source does not mean every statement is supported by every part of it. Link each item under review to the provision that directly supports it. This is practice in matching separate claims to their evidence.

wrong.0: The articles for A and B are reversed.
wrong.2: The articles for B and C are reversed.
wrong.3: The articles for A and C are reversed.

questions.q:
[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
Isotakeshima means Ulleungdo; Matsushima means Dokdo. Fukuura is a place on Dogo in the Oki Islands.

Convert "Fukuura -> Matsushima -> Isotakeshima" into modern island names, starting with the island group containing the departure point.
questions.fact: The modern-name sequence is [[Oki Islands / Dokdo / Ulleungdo]].
blankDistractors: Ulleungdo, Dokdo and the Oki Islands
Dokdo, the Oki Islands and Ulleungdo
questions.explain: Use the supplied name equivalents: Fukuura is in Oki, Matsushima is Dokdo, and Isotakeshima is Ulleungdo.
questions.deep: Historical place names do not necessarily match present usage. This exercise uses the identifications in the commentary for one particular map. It does not authorize applying the same name table to every map from every period without checking.

wrong.0: The names for the two islands are reversed.
wrong.1: The departure point and final destination are reversed.
wrong.3: This incorrectly places Fukuura on Dokdo.

questions.q:
[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
Recorded distances: Dokdo to Ulleungdo about 40 ri; Fukuura to Dokdo about 80 ri. These are historical map figures, not modern measurements.

What is the simplest whole-number ratio of the two recorded distances, in that order?
questions.fact: The ratio of 40 ri to 80 ri is [[1:2]].
questions.explain: Both values use the same unit. Divide both parts of 40:80 by 40 to obtain 1:2.
questions.deep: Follow the order requested when calculating a ratio. The result compares figures recorded on an old map. It does not mean modern route lengths or sailing times have the same ratio.

wrong.0: This reverses the requested order.
wrong.1: This uses the sum of the distances as the second value.
wrong.2: The recorded distances are not equal.

questions.q:
[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
The recorded Dokdo-to-Ulleungdo distance is about 40 ri. The commentary uses 1 ri as approximately 3.9 km.

Convert the historical figure, not the modern measured distance. What is about 40 ri using this conversion?
questions.fact: Converting 40 ri at about 3.9 km per ri gives about [[156 km]].
questions.explain: 40 x 3.9 = 156 km. This converts the old map's figure; it is not the modern measured distance between the islands.
questions.deep: Converting an old unit and testing the accuracy of an old record are different tasks. A unit conversion does not remove errors in the original measurement. Label the result as a conversion of the historical figure.

wrong.1: This loses one decimal place in multiplication.
wrong.2: This converts 80 ri instead.
wrong.3: This divides 40 by 3.9 instead of multiplying.

questions.q:
[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
Recorded segments: Fukuura to Dokdo about 80 ri; Dokdo to Ulleungdo about 40 ri. These are historical map values.

Add the two consecutive segments. What total is recorded for the route?
questions.fact: Adding the historical segments of 80 ri and 40 ri gives about [[120 ri]].
questions.explain: 80 + 40 = 120 ri. A two-segment route is different from the straight-line distance between its endpoints.
questions.deep: A route through several segments has the sum of their lengths. This is not necessarily the direct distance between the start and finish. The exercise calculates old recorded values; it does not reconstruct an actual sailing route.

wrong.0: This uses only the shorter segment.
wrong.2: This uses only the longer segment.
wrong.3: This counts the 80-ri segment twice.

[Source: National Institute of Korean History commentary on the Isotakeshima sketch map]
From Dokdo, Ulleungdo is to the northwest.

Reverse the reference point: from Ulleungdo, in which direction is Dokdo?
questions.fact: Reversing the stated northwest relation places Dokdo [[southeast]] of Ulleungdo.
questions.explain: Reversing the endpoints changes north to south and west to east. The opposite of northwest is southeast.
questions.deep: A direction depends on the reference point. Reusing the original direction after exchanging the start and destination reverses their relation incorrectly. This reads a compass relationship from the commentary, not an actual navigational bearing.

wrong.0: This keeps the original direction despite changing the reference point.
wrong.1: The north-south component has not been reversed.
wrong.3: The east-west component has not been reversed.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Articles 3 and 57: territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles and EEZ outer limit up to 200 nautical miles, both measured from the same baseline.
[Assumption] Ignore overlapping national claims; this does not determine actual boundaries around Dokdo.

An officer adds 200 miles beyond a 12-mile territorial sea. At what distance from the baseline should the EEZ limit instead be drawn?
questions.fact: The EEZ maximum is measured from the same baseline at [[200 nautical miles]], without adding the 12-mile territorial sea.
questions.explain: Both limits are measured from the baseline. The EEZ maximum is not 200 miles beyond the territorial sea's outer edge.
questions.deep: Check the starting point before adding distances from different provisions. This is a hypothetical application of a general maximum. It does not determine actual delimitation or any particular island's maritime entitlement.

wrong.0: This counts the territorial-sea width twice.
wrong.1: The baseline, not the territorial-sea boundary, is the reference point.
wrong.2: This wrongly adds the contiguous-zone maximum.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Articles 3, 33 and 57: maxima from the same baseline are territorial sea 12, contiguous-zone outer limit 24 and EEZ outer limit 200 nautical miles.
[Assumption] Test only these distance ceilings, not actual delimitation.

Plans, in the order above: A=(10,24,190), B=(14,24,190), C=(10,26,190), D=(10,24,210). Which meets all three ceilings?
questions.fact: Of the four hypothetical plans, [[Plan A]] alone meets all three distance ceilings.
questions.explain: Only A stays within all three maxima. Meeting these distance limits does not mean that every other legal requirement is satisfied.
questions.deep: A maximum is a ceiling, not a value that must always be used. A 10-mile territorial sea or 190-mile EEZ limit is not excluded by these distance conditions alone. Overlap with other states is outside the assumptions.

wrong.1: A 14-mile territorial sea exceeds the 12-mile maximum.
wrong.2: A 26-mile contiguous-zone limit exceeds 24 miles.
wrong.3: A 210-mile EEZ limit exceeds 200 miles.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Articles 3, 33, 55 and 57: the contiguous zone and EEZ lie beyond the territorial sea. Their outer maxima are 24 and 200 nautical miles from the baseline.
[Assumption] No overlap with other states.

Set the territorial sea at 12 miles, contiguous-zone limit at 24 and EEZ limit at 200. Which two distance-based labels can apply together at 18 miles?
questions.fact: With the stated limits, a point 18 miles from the baseline can lie in both the [[contiguous zone and EEZ]].
questions.explain: 18 is beyond 12 but within both 24 and 200. The contiguous zone and EEZ can overlap spatially.
questions.deep: Maritime-zone names do not always denote mutually exclusive strips. Zones with different legal functions can occupy the same space. Spatial overlap does not make every power exercised there identical.

wrong.0: 18 miles is outside the stated territorial sea.
wrong.2: The point can be in the EEZ, but not the territorial sea.
wrong.3: The point is seaward of both the baseline and territorial-sea boundary.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Article 57: the EEZ outer limit cannot exceed 200 nautical miles from the baseline used to measure the territorial sea.

On a teaching scale, not an actual map, the baseline is at 0 cm and 1 cm represents 20 nautical miles. Where should the maximum be marked?
questions.fact: At 20 nautical miles per centimeter, the 200-mile maximum lies at [[10 cm]].
questions.explain: Divide 200 by 20: the mark lies 10 cm from zero.
questions.deep: Divide the total real distance by the distance represented by one centimeter. This teaching scale does not reproduce an actual coastline or baseline. Do not use the calculated position as a real maritime boundary around Dokdo.

wrong.0: This represents only 20 nautical miles.
wrong.1: This represents 100 nautical miles.
wrong.3: This represents 400 nautical miles, twice the maximum.

questions.q:
[Source: summaries of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)]
Article 33: in the contiguous zone, necessary control may prevent or punish infringement of customs, fiscal, immigration or sanitary laws within a state's territory or territorial sea.

[Assumption] A vessel is 18 miles from the baseline, beyond a 12-mile territorial sea. Which purpose directly supports action to prevent smuggling into the state?
questions.fact: The directly relevant Article 33 purpose is [[preventing customs-law infringements]].
blankDistractors: A change in the vessel's nationality
questions.explain: Article 33 permits necessary control to prevent customs-law infringements within the territory or territorial sea. It is not unlimited control over every activity.
questions.deep: Check the purpose and scope of a provision as well as the location. This asks whether the purpose of a measure matches the provision. It does not decide the legality of a particular coercive action against a specific vessel.

wrong.0: This wrongly converts limited control into a power of annexation.
wrong.1: This is not the control purpose stated in the article.
wrong.2: Necessary control is different from an unconditional blanket ban.

questions.q: Which document issued by the Meiji government's Foreign Ministry in 1870 described Ulleungdo and Dokdo as dependencies of Joseon?
questions.fact: The circumstances in which Ulleungdo and Dokdo became dependencies of Joseon appear in the 1870 [[Chosengoku Kosai Shimatsu Naitansho]].
questions.explain: The Meiji Foreign Ministry prepared this report in 1870. A separate heading describes how the two islands became dependencies of Joseon, seven years before the Dajokan Directive.
questions.deep: The document's title, Chosengoku Kosai Shimatsu Naitansho, means a confidential report on relations with Joseon. In 1870, soon after the Meiji government was established, the Foreign Ministry sent officials to investigate conditions in Joseon. The report includes a separate section on how Ulleungdo and Dokdo became dependencies of Joseon. The important point is that the heading itself treats the two islands as dependencies of Joseon. Japanese officials carried out the investigation and wrote the report. Its timing matters: seven years before the 1877 Dajokan Directive and 35 years before Japan's 1905 incorporation claim. Japan described Dokdo as ownerless in 1905, although its own Foreign Ministry had associated the island with Joseon a generation earlier. Question #099, on the same fact, had a correct-answer rate of only 20%. The Dajokan Directive is better known; this report is less familiar.

wrong.0: The Dajokan Directive dates to 1877, seven years later.
wrong.1: Onshu Shicho Goki is a Japanese geography book from 1667, over 200 years earlier.
wrong.3: Shimane Notice No. 40 claimed incorporation in 1905, a very different purpose.

questions.q: Which Japanese person was executed in 1837 after violating the ban on travel to Ulleungdo?
questions.fact: In 1837, Hachiemon received [[the death penalty]] for illegally traveling to Ulleungdo.
questions.explain: The ban first issued in 1696 remained in force. Hachiemon's execution shows that it was enforced, not merely written down.
questions.deep: Hachiemon was a merchant from Hamada in Iwami Province, now part of Shimane Prefecture. He went to Ulleungdo in 1836 to cut timber and trade. After discovery, he was tried and executed in 1837. The case is important for its attached map as well as its punishment. Japan is yellow; Joseon's Ulleungdo and Dokdo are red. The court records thus distinguish the islands visually. The source interprets the severe punishment as showing how seriously the shogunate treated the ban on crossing to these islands. The 1696 ban was still being enforced 141 years later. A qualification is essential: the charges concerned violation of the travel ban and illicit trade. The punishment alone does not settle sovereignty. It must be read with the map and the wider historical context.

wrong.0: Nakai petitioned for incorporation in 1905, about 70 years later.
wrong.2: The Murakami family kept records of An Yong-bok's visit to the Oki Islands.
wrong.3: The Oya family received passage permission in the seventeenth century.
